title: What Claude writes down in the repo

items.scenario: Eighteen months after a refund-rounding fix, an auditor asks why rounding happens after currency conversion. The commit message says only 'fix rounding'.
items.question: Which artefact should have captured the answer?
options: A note about rounding in the project CLAUDE.md
A worklog entry for that fix, linked from the commit
Claude's auto memory on the original developer's laptop
A MISTAKES.md entry written by Claude
items.explanation: A worklog entry records the symptom, what was investigated, what was rejected and why, and what was chosen — exactly the 'why' a later reader needs.
distractors: CLAUDE.md holds standing instructions, not the history of a fix.
Auto memory is machine-local, unreviewed and not a record; it may not even exist anymore.
MISTAKES.md is for human corrections, and Claude doesn't write to it.

items.scenario: A developer proposes committing ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/MEMORY.md into the repo so the team shares what Claude has learned.
items.question: What is the right response?
options: Commit it; shared memory keeps everyone's sessions consistent across machines
Commit it, but have Claude regenerate it from scratch every week
Don't commit it; promote true, useful notes into CLAUDE.md or rules
Paste its contents into the README so humans can read it too
items.explanation: Auto memory is per-machine, unreviewed and self-contradicting. The right path is to promote reviewed, stable facts into committed instructions.
distractors: It turns unreviewed guesses into shared instructions without review.
Regenerating it doesn't make it reviewed or consistent.
Moving unreviewed notes into another file doesn't fix that nobody checked them.

items.scenario: A worklog entry from last month turns out to be wrong about the root cause. A teammate wants to edit the entry to fix it.
items.question: What is the convention?
options: Edit the old entry so readers only see the correct version
Delete the old entry to avoid confusion
Move the old entry to an archive folder
Append a new entry that corrects it and links back
items.explanation: The worklog is append-only: an edited record can't be trusted. Corrections are new entries that reference the old one.
distractors: Silent edits destroy the trustworthiness of the whole log.
Deletion loses the history of what was believed and why.
Archiving hides the error without recording the correction.

items.scenario: The team decides all services must publish domain events through a transactional outbox. A developer writes it up as a worklog entry.
items.question: Where should this decision live, and why?
options: In an ADR, because it binds future work
In the worklog, because it was decided this week
In MISTAKES.md, because the old approach lost events
Only in the PR description that introduced it
items.explanation: An ADR binds future work; a worklog explains past work. A rule that constrains all future services is an ADR, with deciders named.
distractors: A worklog entry explains a past fix; it doesn't carry decision status or bind future changes.
MISTAKES.md records corrections to Claude's work, not architecture decisions.
PR descriptions are hard to find later and have no status or supersede mechanism.

items.scenario: Two years after ADR-0004 chose Kafka, the team moves to a managed queue. Someone suggests deleting ADR-0004 to avoid confusing new joiners.
items.question: What should happen to ADR-0004?
options: Delete it and renumber the remaining ADRs
Edit it to describe the new queue instead
Mark it superseded by the new ADR, which links back
Leave it unchanged and add a note about the new queue to CLAUDE.md
items.explanation: ADRs are superseded, not deleted. The record of why the team changed its mind is part of the history.
distractors: Deleting and renumbering breaks references and loses history.
Rewriting an accepted ADR falsifies the original decision.
An unchanged ADR still reads as current; the status must change.

items.scenario: To be helpful, Claude has started adding entries to MISTAKES.md whenever it notices it made an error.
items.question: Why is this a problem?
options: Claude should log its errors in auto memory instead
Its value is human judgement; Claude can't log errors it didn't notice
MISTAKES.md must be generated automatically by a hook, not written by Claude
It's fine as long as a human reads the file weekly
items.explanation: MISTAKES.md is human corrections only. Its value is a human's judgement that something was wrong, which by definition includes the errors Claude didn't notice.
distractors: Moving the log doesn't fix the problem: self-noticed errors aren't the content, and auto memory is unreviewed and local.
Hook-generated content is the anti-pattern this module warns against.
Reading doesn't change that the entries reflect only Claude's self-detected errors.

items.scenario: A repo has plan.md files from three features. In one, the implementation changed approach mid-way and plan.md was never updated.
items.question: What is the risk, and the fix?
options: No real risk; plan.md is a draft and the code is the truth
Delete all plan.md files from the repository so they can never drift
Leave it as is; the worklog entries will explain the difference eventually
A stale plan misleads; update it in the same PR or record the deviation
items.explanation: A plan.md that no longer matches the code is worse than none. Keep it honest in the same PR, or record the deviation in the worklog.
distractors: Committed plans are part of the audit trail readers trust; a draft that looks authoritative misleads.
Deleting them throws away the reasoning the trail exists to keep.
An unlinked future note doesn't stop readers being misled by the plan now.

items.scenario: A new teammate's PR includes CLAUDE.local.md with their personal paths and a .claude/settings.local.json they created by hand.
items.question: What should the repo do?
options: Accept both; Claude in CI then gets the same setup as the author
Ignore both in the repo .gitignore and remove them from the PR
Accept the settings file but ignore CLAUDE.local.md
Rename both to CLAUDE.md and settings.json so the team shares them
items.explanation: Both are personal, machine-local files. Add them to the repository .gitignore so every clone is protected, rather than relying on per-user global excludes.
distractors: Personal paths and local settings don't belong in a shared repo, may leak details, and won't match CI's environment anyway.
settings.local.json is personal by design and shouldn't be committed either.
Turning personal preferences into shared instructions bypasses review of what the team wants.

items.scenario: After a team adds a hook that forces a worklog file on every commit, the repo has 900 entries in three months, most reading 'Symptom: n/a'.
items.question: What is the best correction?
options: Keep the hook but have Claude write longer, more detailed entries
Drop the per-commit hook; require entries for judgement calls in PR review
Delete docs/worklog/ and rely on commit messages for the why
Move the entries into CLAUDE.md so Claude reads them every session
items.explanation: Documentation generated because a hook required it is the named anti-pattern. Entries are for fixes and judgement calls, reviewed like code.
distractors: Longer filler is still filler; volume without value.
Losing the worklog removes the record for the cases that matter; commit messages can't hold rejected options and uncertainty.
That bloats CLAUDE.md with history, the failure mode the five-artefact split prevents.

items.scenario: A client's compliance team asks you to show how AI-assisted changes to their codebase were controlled over the engagement.
items.question: Which evidence best answers them?
options: Exported chat transcripts from developers' Claude sessions
Each developer's auto memory files, exported at engagement end
A signed statement from the tech lead that Claude Code was configured securely throughout
Committed intent/spec/plan, reviewed diffs, and worklog entries naming reviewers
items.explanation: The committed record shows reasoning, approval points and named human reviewers for each change — reconstructable from the repo alone.
distractors: Transcripts are scattered, may not be retained, and don't show review or approval.
Auto memory is unreviewed private scratch, not evidence of control.
An assertion isn't evidence.
